content.thinking:
I need to be precise about timing here: the flag was reverted at 15:25:00, but the service wasn't back at baseline by that check, and the user independently resolved things at 15:25:08 while keeping the flag off. Since metrics show recovery exactly at 15:25:08, I should classify the revert action as withdrawn rather than claim it fixed the issue.

There's also a timing discrepancy worth flagging — the flag toggle event is recorded at 15:24:52, but errors began at 15:19, and flag evaluation logs show it partially on at that earlier time. This suggests the recorded toggle timestamp might just mark the final switch rather than when rollout actually started, so I'll note that as an assumption rather than a fact. I also want to avoid stating specific figures like line numbers when referencing file locations in the error trace.

Chaining the causal story: account page requests failed for a subset of shoppers, those requests hit a ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code, and that code path only ran because the monthly-spend-feature flag was rolling out to a growing share of evaluations. The root cause stops at the flag exposing an unsafe divide-by-zero path — why the code lacks a guard isn't something the record explains. Contributing factors include the fast rollout from zero to full with no staged halt, and detection lagged the actual onset by several minutes, so I want to call out test coverage for the zero case, staged rollout with auto-halt, and faster alerting as action items.

I'm also noting the flag change wasn't reflected in the change feed in time for investigators, and that resolution relied on a human catching it rather than an automated rollback. So I'm drafting a numbered action item list: fixing the division-by-zero bug with a test, adding staged rollout gating, lowering the alert threshold for earlier detection, and ensuring flag changes get logged promptly in the change feed — with one more process item still to define.

For the lessons section, I'm capturing what went well (quick investigation via logs, cheap flag revert), what went wrong (verdict withdrawal timing, noisy disconnect errors), and what got lucky (the failure stayed contained to the flag-gated path). Then I'll move on to drafting the executive summary with the duration and other key figures filled in.

action_items.item: Fix the division by zero in the spend summary code on the account page, add a test for the zero-denominator case, and only then turn monthly-spend-feature back on.
Roll feature flags out in stages, such as a small share of traffic first, with automatic rollback or a halt when the account page error rate rises above baseline.
Review the HighErrorRate alert so a sustained rise in account page errors pages sooner after the onset, for example with a shorter evaluation window or a lower threshold on that page.
Record flag changes in the change feed at the moment the rollout begins, with the percentage, so the Investigator sees them when it looks for changes before the alert.

Make the Mitigation Agent's verification wait long enough for per-minute metrics to reflect the action, and reconcile its verdict with a human resolution so that a revert that was kept is recorded as such.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers opening the account page got errors. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, and the account-page failure log lines and the warning about account page error rate appear from the onset.

The failing requests raised a ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code (spend_summary.py). Other errors in the logs were shoppers closing the connection, which is background noise and not the cause.

That code ran because the flag monthly-spend-feature was turned on. Flag evaluations were mostly off just before the onset, then partly on at the onset, then fully on afterwards, in step with the error rise. Latency, CPU and memory stayed flat, which points away from a resource or traffic problem.

The flag enabled a code path that divides by zero for some requests, and nothing guarded that division or halted the rollout when the error rate rose. The record stops here: it does not show which input is zero or why the code shipped without a check.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend summary code path had no protection against a zero denominator and no test covering it, so enabling the flag exposed a defect that had never run under real traffic.
The flag moved from off to fully on within a short window with no staged rollout and no automatic halt or rollback on a rising error rate, so many shoppers were affected before anyone acted.
The page came late. The alert was raised well after the onset, so the incident was already underway for several minutes before Argus took it up.

The flag change is recorded in the change feed with a timestamp after the onset, and the change lookup for the period before the alert returned no production changes. The flag history and logs had to supply the link between flag and errors.

The mitigation check ran before the metrics could show recovery, and a person resolved the incident while the action was still unconfirmed, leaving the verdict as withdrawn even though the flag stayed off and the service recovered.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, starting at {began}, a share of shoppers got errors when opening their account page. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. A newly enabled feature, a monthly spend summary, hit a division-by-zero bug. Argus found the flag change as the leading cause and switched the flag off. A person then marked the incident resolved and kept the flag off, and the metrics show recovery by {recovered}. Argus's own checks right after the revert had not yet seen a return to baseline, so it judged its action withdrawn. The recovery coincides with the revert but was not confirmed by Argus. The shopper-facing fault is gone while the flag stays off, and the underlying bug is not yet fixed.

got_lucky: The faulty path sat behind a flag, so turning it off was a one-step mitigation. A bug in code with no flag would have needed a deploy.
The record gives no sign that the failure spread beyond the account page.
went_well: The Investigator read metrics, logs, change events and flag history and named the flag as the leading cause with a specific error and file.
The mitigation was a cheap, reversible flag revert, and the human kept the flag off and told the checkout team.
Argus took the incident up within seconds of the alert.
went_wrong: The error rate had been elevated for several minutes before the alert fired.
The change lookup before the alert found no production changes, because the flag change was recorded after the onset.
The action was judged withdrawn because the check ran before recovery showed, so Argus never confirmed that the revert fixed it.
The bug itself is still in the code, so re-enabling the flag would bring the errors back.

input.root_cause: Switching on the feature flag monthly-spend-feature exposed shoppers to a spend-summary code path on the account page that raises a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py. The code was enabled for a growing share of traffic with nothing to guard the divide or stop the rollout when errors rose. The record does not show which input produces the zero.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for some shoppers
